job.style: a description of a classroom activity or experiment and what it shows

passage: Today in our science class, we examined various food packets to understand how to read labels correctly. We started by looking at a box of cookies that claimed 'No added sugar' on the front, but the ingredient list clearly showed 'maltose' and 'fruit juice concentrate', which are forms of sugar. We learned that the first ingredient listed is always the one present in the largest quantity by weight. Next, we compared two packets of snacks. One had a green dot, confirming it is vegetarian, while the other had no mark at all. Our teacher explained that a missing mark does not automatically mean a product is vegetarian; one must always check the full ingredient list. We also discussed the FSSAI logo, which is a regulatory mark indicating that the food meets safety standards, not necessarily that the product is 'healthy' or nutritious. Finally, we looked at a bottle of juice with a 'Best Before' date. We learned that 'Best Before' indicates the quality and freshness period, whereas an 'Expiry' date indicates the point after which food may become unsafe to consume. We concluded that reading the fine print is essential for making informed choices, as marketing claims on the front of the pack can often be misleading.

items.evidence: We started by looking at a box of cookies that claimed 'No added sugar' on the front, but the ingredient list clearly showed 'maltose' and 'fruit juice concentrate', which are forms of sugar.
items.q: A cookie box says 'No added sugar', but its ingredients include maltose. What should a careful reader conclude?
options: The cookies still have sweeteners under other names
The cookies have no sugar, as 'sugar' is not listed
The cookies are sugar-free, as the front label says
The cookies contain a harmful chemical called maltose
items.explain: Maltose and fruit juice concentrate are forms of sugar, so the cookies still contain sugar despite the front claim.

wrong.why: thinks only the word 'sugar' means sugar is present
trusts the marketing claim on the front of the pack
thinks unfamiliar ingredient names are harmful chemicals

items.evidence: We learned that the first ingredient listed is always the one present in the largest quantity by weight.
items.q: A biscuit label lists: wheat flour, sugar, palm oil, salt. Which ingredient is present in the greatest amount?
options: Wheat flour, since it is listed first
Salt, since the last item is the largest
Sugar, since biscuits are mostly sugar
All four equally, as the order means nothing
items.explain: The first ingredient listed is always present in the largest quantity by weight, so wheat flour is the most.

wrong.why: thinks the first ingredient is the smallest, so the last is largest
guesses from taste instead of reading the order
does not know the order of ingredients has meaning

items.evidence: Our teacher explained that a missing mark does not automatically mean a product is vegetarian; one must always check the full ingredient list.
items.q: A vegetarian student finds a snack packet with no green or brown mark. What should the student do?
options: Check every ingredient listed to decide
Treat it as vegetarian because it has no mark
Trust the FSSAI logo to show it is vegetarian
Check the Best Before date to decide
items.explain: A missing mark does not mean a product is vegetarian, so you must always check the full ingredient list.

wrong.why: thinks food without a mark is vegetarian
thinks the FSSAI logo tells you everything good about the food
picks a different label detail from the passage

items.evidence: We also discussed the FSSAI logo, which is a regulatory mark indicating that the food meets safety standards, not necessarily that the product is 'healthy' or nutritious.
items.q: Meena says a chips packet with the FSSAI logo must be good for her. What does the logo really tell her?
options: The food has met official safety rules
The food is nutritious and good for health
The food has no chemicals or additives
The food shares one licence with all brands
items.explain: The FSSAI logo means the food meets safety standards; it does not mean the food is healthy or nutritious.

wrong.why: thinks an FSSAI logo means the food is healthy
mixes up the logo with having no additives
thinks the FSSAI licence is the same on all products

items.evidence: We learned that 'Best Before' indicates the quality and freshness period, whereas an 'Expiry' date indicates the point after which food may become unsafe to consume.
items.q: How is a 'Best Before' date different from an 'Expiry' date?
options: Best Before is about quality; Expiry is about safety
Best Before is about safety; Expiry is about quality
Best Before and Expiry both mark unsafe food
Best Before is for drinks; Expiry is for snacks
items.explain: Best Before shows how long food stays fresh and good; Expiry shows when it may become unsafe to eat.

wrong.why: swaps the meanings of the two dates
thinks the two dates mean the same thing
turns the juice bottle example into a rule
